### RNA-seq count and meta data from TCGA-BRCA cohort

## Outline - 

## 1. Data Preparation 

## 2. Gene selection and summary statistics

## 1. Data Preparation

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(plotly)# load packages
```

```{r} 
# Import data 
counts <- read.csv("counts.csv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
# Initially did not use check.names = FALSE, which caused problems when combining with metadata 
# read.csv() changed the hyphens to periods in the column names of counts

metadata <- read.csv("meta_data.csv", row.names = 1)

## Counts - gene-expression count - the numbers represent how many sequencing reads/fragments
# were assigned to the RNA transcripts from those genes
# Higher RNA-seq count generally means more RNA from that gene was detected → higher gene expression
## Meta data - Information describing each sample/patient

```

```{r}
# Inspect data
dim(counts)
dim(metadata)

# head(counts)
head(metadata)

colnames(counts)
colnames(metadata)
```

## 2. Gene Selection and Summary Statistics

### 2a. ERBB2 Gene Selection and Summary Statistics

```{r}

# I see a lot of pneumotoxicity from ENHERTU which has a targeted antibody used to treat HER-2+ breast CA 
# The gene ERBB2 codes for HER-2 so I looked up the Ensembl ID for ERBB2 and found it to be ENSG00000141736
# But Ensembl IDs have version suffixes ENSG00000141736.XX so had to use grep() to find it 

# Select ERBB2 gene 
grep("ENSG00000141736", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # Used ChatGPTs assistance to learn grep()

ERBB2_data <- counts["ENSG00000141736.14", ] # from the data frame of counts, 
# I'm selecting the row with my gene of interest
head(ERBB2_data)
dim(ERBB2_data)

# Transpose 
ERBB2_data <- t(ERBB2_data) # transpose the data 
head(ERBB2_data)
dim(ERBB2_data)

# Rename the column
colnames(ERBB2_data) <- "ERBB2"
head(ERBB2_data)
dim(ERBB2_data)
class(ERBB2_data)

# Change matrix to data frame 
ERBB2_data_df <- as.data.frame(ERBB2_data)
head(ERBB2_data_df)

# Convert to tibble 
ERBB2_data_tbl <- tibble(ERBB2_data_df) 

head (ERBB2_data_tbl)

# Summary statistics
ERBB2_summary <- ERBB2_data_tbl %>%
  summarize(
    mean = mean(ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE), 
    sd = sd(ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

ERBB2_summary

```

### 2b. Covariate Summary Statistics

```{r}

# Choose one covariate from metadata 
colnames(metadata) # the molecular BRCA subtype seems the most relevant to me

# PAM50 looks at the RNA expression pattern of 50 genes and 
# uses that pattern to classify tumors into molecular subtypes

PAM50_counts <- table(metadata$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50) # identify categories in this group 
# Used ChatGPT's assistance to learn table()
PAM50_counts

# Calculate percentage of subtypes
PAM50_percent <- PAM50_counts / sum(PAM50_counts) * 100
PAM50_percent

# Combine in a data frame 
PAM50_summary <- data.frame(
  Subtype = names(PAM50_counts),
  Count = as.numeric(PAM50_counts),
  Percent = round(as.numeric(PAM50_percent), 1) # round to one decimal place 
)

PAM50_summary

# Create PAM50 table 

PAM50_table <- data.frame(
  Covariate = "PAM50 subtype",
  Statistic = paste(PAM50_summary$Subtype, "n (%)"),
  Value = paste0(
    PAM50_summary$Count,
    " (",
    PAM50_summary$Percent,
    "%)"
  )
)

PAM50_table


# Choose age at initial pathologic diagnosis as the second covariate
summary(metadata$paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis)

# Check the variable type
class(metadata$paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis)

# Check for missing values
sum(is.na(metadata$paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis))

# Calculate summary statistics for age at initial pathologic diagnosis

age_summary <- metadata %>%
  summarize(
    mean = mean(paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, na.rm = TRUE),
    max = max(paper_age_at_initial_pathologic_diagnosis, na.rm = TRUE)
  )

age_summary

# Create age table 

age_table <- data.frame(
  Covariate = "Age at initial pathologic diagnosis",
  Statistic = c("Mean", "Median", "SD", "Minimum", "Maximum"),
  Value = c(
    round(age_summary$mean, 2),
    age_summary$median,
    round(age_summary$sd, 2),
    age_summary$min,
    age_summary$max
  )
)

age_table

# Combine the covariates 
covariate_summary <- rbind(PAM50_table, age_table)

# Remove repeated covariate names for cleaner table display
covariate_summary$Covariate[c(2:5, 7:10)] <- ""

covariate_summary

```

## 3. Data visualization

### 3a. Histogram — distribution of ERBB2 expression

```{r}

ggplot(
  ERBB2_data_tbl, # data to be used
  aes(x = ERBB2)) + # map variable
  geom_histogram(bins = 30, fill = "blue", alpha = 0.7) + # choose plot
  
  # add mean and median lines based on peer feedback
geom_vline( 
  xintercept = mean(ERBB2_data_tbl$ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
  linetype = "dashed"
) +
geom_vline( 
  xintercept = median(ERBB2_data_tbl$ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
  linetype = "dotted"
) + 
  # Annotate the mean and median lines
  annotate(
  "text",
  x = mean(ERBB2_data_tbl$ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
  y = Inf, # put the label on top of the plot
  label = "Mean",
  vjust = 1.5 # move it slightly downward
) +
annotate(
  "text",
  x = median(ERBB2_data_tbl$ERBB2, na.rm = TRUE),
  y = Inf,
  label = "Median",
  vjust = 1.5
) +
  scale_x_log10() + # ERBB2 expression is strongly right-skewed, 
# so a log10 scale is used to better visualize the distribution
  labs(
    x = "ERBB2 RNA-seq count (log10 scale)",
    y = "Number of samples",
    title = "Distribution of ERBB2 Gene Expression"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# Used ChatGPT's assistance to learn geom_vline, annotate, & scale_x_log10

```
### 3b. Scatterplot — relationship between ERBB2 and CDK4

```{r}

# Select a second gene - CDK4 gene Ensembl ID ENSG00000135446
grep("ENSG00000135446", rownames(counts), value = TRUE)

head(CDK4_data)

# Change matrix to data frame 
CDK4_data_df <- as.data.frame(CDK4_data)

```

```{r}
# Create a scatter plot 

# Combine the data from both gene data frames 

Two_gene_data_df <- cbind(ERBB2_data_df, CDK4_data_df)
head(Two_gene_data_df)

# Create scatterplot 

scatterplot <- ggplot(Two_gene_data_df, # data to be used 
       aes(x = ERBB2, y = CDK4)) + # map variables
  geom_point(alpha = 0.4, color = "blue") + # choose plot
  geom_smooth(method = "lm") + # add linear regression line based on peer feedback
  scale_x_log10() + # log10 scale is used to better visualize the distribution
  scale_y_log10() +
  labs(x = "ERBB2 RNA-seq count (log10 scale)", # add labels
       y = "CDK4 RNA-seq count (log10 scale)",
       title = "log10-scaled ERBB2 vs. CDK4 Gene Expression") +
  theme_minimal() # customize appearance 
scatterplot

# ggplotly(scatterplot) 

# Most samples cluster within a relatively narrow range of ERBB2 and CDK4 expression
# The log10 scales allow the relationship to be visualized despite the wide range of RNA-seq counts
# The regression line suggests a modest positive relationship between ERBB2 and CDK4 expression

```
### 3c. Violin + box plot — ERBB2 expression across PAM50 subtypes

```{r}

# Merge gene data to metadata 

# row names were a bit different since read.csv() defaults to check.names = TRUE
# hyphens get converted to periods
# went back and switched to counts <- read.csv("counts.csv", row.names = 1, check.names = FALSE)
# Used ChatGPTs assistance to troubleshoot 

ERBB2gene_metadata <- merge(ERBB2_data_df, metadata,
                       by = "row.names",
                       all = TRUE)

head(ERBB2gene_metadata)
dim(ERBB2gene_metadata)

# Clean up merged data frame 

rownames(ERBB2gene_metadata) <- ERBB2gene_metadata$Row.names
# put the sample IDs back into the row names

ERBB2gene_metadata <- subset(ERBB2gene_metadata,
                        select = -c(Row.names))
# remove the now-unnecessary Row.names column.

head(ERBB2gene_metadata)
dim(ERBB2gene_metadata)

# Create violin plot of ERBB2 expression by BRCA PAM50 subtype

ggplot(ERBB2gene_metadata %>%
    filter(!is.na(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)), # filtered out the NA values
       aes(x = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
           y = ERBB2,
           fill = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)) +
  geom_violin() +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.1, fill = "white") + # add box plot based on peer feedback
  labs(
    x = "BRCA PAM50 Breast Cancer Subtype",
    y = "ERBB2 RNA-seq Count (log10 scale)",
    fill = "BRCA PAM50 Subtype",
    title = "ERBB2 Gene Expression by PAM50 Subtype"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  scale_fill_brewer(palette = "Set2") +
  scale_y_log10() # Thanks Paul Skeffington for discussing log scale during the in-class exercises!!

# without the log scale, the right-skewed distributions make
# the distributions near the bottom of violin plot difficult to see
# one option would be to de-lim the y-axis but then you hide the high-expression observations

```
### 3d. Cumulative distribution function — additional new plot type

I chose to create a cumulative distribution function to compare the distribution of ERBB2 expression across PAM50 molecular subtypes and to complement the histogram and violin plot by displaying the cumulative proportion of samples across the range of ERBB2 expression.

```{r}

ggplot(
  ERBB2gene_metadata %>% 
    filter(!is.na(paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)), # filtered out the NA values
  aes(x = ERBB2, color = paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)) + # map variables
  stat_ecdf() + # choose plot
  scale_x_log10() + # log10 scale is used to better visualize the distribution
  labs(
    x = "ERBB2 RNA-seq Count (log10 scale)", # add labels
    y = "Cumulative Proportion",
    color = "BRCA PAM50 Subtype",
    title = "Cumulative Distribution of ERBB2 Expression by PAM50 Subtype"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# The Her2 subtype curve is shifted to the right, indicating higher ERBB2 expression
# Basal samples generally show lower ERBB2 expression
# LumA, LumB, and Normal subtypes show intermediate distributions

```
### 3e. Heatmap — expression patterns across the 10 selected genes with PAM50 annotation

```{r, fig.width=12, fig.height=7}

# load heatmap libraries
library(ComplexHeatmap)
library(circlize)


# Similar to above, in addition to ERBB2 and CDK4, I chose 8 more clinically relevant breast CA genes 
# Use grep() to identify the exact Ensembl IDs for the genes in the dataset 

grep("ENSG00000105810", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # CDK6
grep("ENSG00000091831", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # ESR1
grep("ENSG00000082175", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # PGR
grep("ENSG00000148773", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # MKI67
grep("ENSG00000146648", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # EGFR
grep("ENSG00000186081", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # KRT5
grep("ENSG00000129514", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # FOXA1
grep("ENSG00000107485", rownames(counts), value = TRUE) # GATA3

## Selecting final 10 genes

genes_for_heatmap <- c(
  ERBB2 = "ENSG00000141736.14",
  CDK4  = "ENSG00000135446.17",
  CDK6  = "ENSG00000105810.10",
  ESR1  = "ENSG00000091831.24",
  PGR   = "ENSG00000082175.15",
  MKI67 = "ENSG00000148773.14",
  EGFR  = "ENSG00000146648.19",
  KRT5  = "ENSG00000186081.12",
  FOXA1 = "ENSG00000129514.8",
  GATA3 = "ENSG00000107485.18"
)

genes_for_heatmap
# Thanks to Steve Hutchins for feedback on this step!

## Keep only the 10 genes we want
counts_subset <- counts[genes_for_heatmap, ]
counts_subset <- as.matrix(counts_subset)

# Replace Ensembl IDs with gene symbols
rownames(counts_subset) <- names(genes_for_heatmap)

# Initially I did not do the 2 steps - matrix and log and got both errors 
# 1. Data is not a matrix 
# 2. ComplexHeatmap told me that my raw counts contain some very large values -
# hence few of the huge counts could dominate the colors and hide patterns in the rest of the data
# Used ChatGPT to assist with these 

# log2(counts_subset + 1) is a common transformation used with RNA-seq count data
# to reduce skewness and compress the large numerical range

# Log transform counts
counts_subset_log <- log2(counts_subset + 1)

table(metadata$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50)

## Heatmap annotations
column_ha <- HeatmapAnnotation(
  PAM50 = metadata$paper_BRCA_Subtype_PAM50,
  col = list(
    PAM50 = c(
      Basal = "red",
      Her2 = "blue",
      LumA = "green",
      LumB = "purple",
      Normal = "yellow"
    )
  )
)

# Create heatmap
Heatmap(
  counts_subset_log,
  name = "log2 Count",
  top_annotation = column_ha,
  show_row_names = TRUE,
  show_column_names = FALSE,
  cluster_columns = TRUE,
  cluster_rows = TRUE,
  column_title = "Samples",
  row_title = "Genes",
  heatmap_legend_param = list(title = "log2 Count")
)
```
